rv.q: I'd say strain every nerve and sinew to bag a ticket to the funniest double-act stage comedy since the Right Size's early Noughties tribute to Morecambe and Wise, The Play What I Wrote.
So it is a considerable pleasure to report that The Comeback could be subtitled 'It, Pretty Much, Spot On', such is the dizzying adroitness of its meta-theatrical capers.

Announcing it earlier this autumn, producer Sonia Friedman hailed this show as “the cure for theatre”. But theatre is still contagious as far as the government is concerned – and The Comeback’s opening performances are to be its last, for a while.
Ashenden and Owen have recently been running needle-sharp spoof zooms on Twitter, having proved that BBC Radio 4 comedy really can be funny with their show The Pin.

The show, which has been developed and expanded in the two years since it was a runaway hit at the Edinburgh Fringe, is built around a clever notion: a lowly double act are providing a warm-up act on a comeback tour by a traditional variety duo, Jimmy and Sid. Ashenden and Owen play both teams.
Their punchlines are all subverted expectations and deliberate anti-climaxes, wryly satisfying but too arch and insubstantial to ever earn a belly laugh.
It's all an inch away from chaos and, since it's perfectly timed and ruthlessly controlled, uproariously funny.
But for the most part it is clever and marvellously warm-hearted, full of surreal joy in what makes people laugh.
Things get very silly, which the audience finds hilarious. It needs ratcheting up higher to make that really work, but there's delightful fun here.

First seen on the Edinburgh Festival fringe, the current sketch show casts its two young performers, Ben Ashenden and Alex Owen, as – you guessed it! – Ben and Alex, who are there to lend support to a veteran comic duo, Jimmy and Sid, who are also played by the show’s two authors.
I have no doubt The Comeback has the ability to leave audiences chuckling for hours, but perhaps not for days.

cn.t: The Pin's West End debut earns enthusiastic praise as a clever, high-energy backstage farce that playfully riffs on theatrical conventions and double-act dynamics with sharp comic timing and infectious fun.
